title: Set-up
text:
Choosing your dataset
In this workshop, you have the option of working with your own data, or an example dataset from Kara Reardon’s research.

Using your own data
If you want to use your own data, have your .fastq.gz reads ready and make a metadata file that describes each of your samples (including key variables). Make sure this data file is tidy.












Kara’s compost tea experiment
If you want to use Kara’s compost tea data, you can download the following:

Sequencing reads (.fastq.gz)
A metadata table: metadata.txt

This project is about compost teas (liquid fertilizers made by brewing organic material in water) and compares how different methods for making diverse agricultural probiotics affect microbiome composition. With Kara’s dataset, we will investigate if there are any differences between bacterial communities in experimental compost teas brewed in the Bell lab.
This experiment contains four treatments:

Inoculant Source
Oxygen Level
Nutrient Source
Steep Time

There are four replicates of each treatment combination (n=312).

title: Data exploration & quality control
text:
The ASV table
The ASV table is the occurrence or abundance table that contains counts corresponding to the number of times each ASV is observed in each sample.
The ASV table has samples in rows and variables (ASVs) in columns.
This is the asv_count.df table from our raw data. We can get the same information from a phyloseq object using the otu_table() function.

Check the first few rows of the OTU table

#check how the raw OTU table looks in the first five rows and first 6 columns
asv_count.df[1:5, 1:6]

#we can also do this with our phyloseq object
otu_table(ps)[1:5, 1:6]



Check the total number of reads

#check the total number of sequences/reads in the OTU table
sum(asv_count.df)



Check the number of samples & ASVs

#check the number of samples (i.e., rows) in the OTU table
dim(asv_count.df)[1] 

#check the number of ASVs (i.e., columns) in the OTU table
dim(asv_count.df)[2]

#we can also do this with our phyloseq object
nsamples(ps)
ntaxa(ps) 



KR: Making adjustments
Some adjustments are necessary to make sure the tables align as follows:

ASV: rows = sample names, columns = ASV number
Taxonomy: rows = ASV number, columns = Kingdom -> Species; clear NA classifications


## ASV
# If rows are NOT sample names, transpose table. Uncomment if needed.
# asv_count.df <- t(asv_count.df)

## Taxonomy
# visualize 
str(taxa.df)
head(taxa.df)
# adjust
rownames(taxa.df) <- taxa.df[,1]  # Set ASV ID as rownames
taxa.df <- taxa.df[,-c(1,1)]
taxa.df[taxa.df == "" | is.na(taxa.df)] <- "unclassified"

## Metadata - align order based on ASV table?


Removing contaminants

unclassified.taxa <- subset(taxa.df, Phylum == "unclassified")
mitochondria.taxa <- subset(taxa.df, Family == "Mitochondria")
archaea.taxa <- subset(taxa.df, Kingdom == "Archaea")
chloroplast.taxa <- subset(taxa.df, Order == "Chloroplast")

un.1<-union(rownames(unclassified.taxa),rownames(mitochondria.taxa))
un.2<-union(rownames(archaea.taxa),un.1)
un.3<-union(rownames(chloroplast.taxa),un.2)

decontaminated.taxa.df <- taxa.df[-which(rownames(taxa.df) %in% un.3),]



Align tables

# Match ASV table with new taxonomy adjusted
adjusted_asv_count.df<-asv_count.df[,which(colnames(asv_count.df) %in% rownames(decontaminated.taxa.df))]

# Match metadata table with reduced ASV table
adjusted_metadata.df <-metadata.df[which(rownames(metadata.df) %in% rownames(adjusted_asv_count.df)),]



Sample read number

rowSums(red.asv) # number of reads per sample
min(rowSums(red.asv)) # minimum reads per sample



Histogram of mean number of reads per sample

sample.sums.filt <- rowSums(red.asv)
summary(sample.sums.filt)
hist(sample.sums.filt, breaks = 50, main = "Read Depth per Sample", xlab = "Total Reads")



Remove samples with zero-reads
Check this step to see if any samples have zero-reads, if not, move-on.

noze.asv <- red.asv[rowSums(red.asv) > 0, ]
lib_sizes <- rowSums(noze.asv)
lib_sizes[lib_sizes == 0]
min(lib_sizes)




Rarefaction Curve
Rarefying is a method of normalization. This step allows for visualization of ASV richness across sampling depths. The key for interpreting this curve, is to identify where ASV richness plateaus. This means that more diversity is not being captured even as sequencing depth increases. The point of plateau can serve as the cutoff normalization where the maximum amount of ASV diversity is kept while prioritizing even sequence depth across samples for downstream processing. Rarefying is ideal for beta diversity analyses.

rarecurve(red.asv, step = 1000, sample = min(rowSums(red.asv)),
          col = "blue", label = FALSE, main = "Rarefaction Curves for All Samples")



Rarefy Samples

set.seed(137) # random number generator, choose 3 digit number so that rarefaction is repeatable
sum(lib_sizes >= 3000) # how many samples have above 3000 reads?
raref.asv <- rrarefy(red.asv,3000)

# Align metadata table with rarefied asv table
raref.metadat<- red.metadat[rownames(raref.asv), ]
# Align taxonomy table with rarefied asv table ??



Relative Abundance
Relative Abundance is another normalization method. This step processes data as a proportion.

# Convert OTU numbers to percentages
asv.perc<-raref.asv/rowSums(raref.asv)*100
rowSums(asv.perc)

asv.table1 <- as.data.frame(asv.perc)
asv.table2 <- t(asv.table1)
asv.table <- as.data.frame(asv.table2)

Negative and Positive Controls

Negative Controls
It is important to include negative controls throughout the extraction and amplification process. These can include blank samples that go through the extraction process, and no-template controls that go through the amplification process. These negatives can then be used to ensure these steps are not amplifying unwanted DNA from the laboratory environment

View(asv.table2) # Sample names as columns


Scroll to BLANK or NEG samples
Order from high to low to see counts for most abundant ASVs
Interpret:


Reads should be below 1000 per ASV
Sample should contain less than 100 different ASVs
If higher than these benchmarks, this could be problematic for interpreting ASVs in actual samples and further steps should be taken to account for these ASVs

title: Data exploration & quality control
text:
Packages for Microbiome Analysis

Phyloseq
Introduce Phyloseq Object and how to check

# Convert dataframes to matrices
asv.matrix <- as.matrix(asv.table)
taxon.matrix <- as.matrix(red.taxon)


# Load Phyloseq
physeq <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(asv.matrix, taxa_are_rows = TRUE),
  tax_table(taxon.matrix),
  sample_data(raref.metadat))


#Align sample names in phyloseq with metadata
metadat.physeq <- raref.metadat[sample_names(physeq), ]


identical(taxa_names(physeq), rownames(tax_table(physeq))) # should be TRUE
identical(sample_names(physeq), rownames(metadat.physeq)) # should be TRUE

# Other checks
head(rownames(otu_table(physeq)))
any(is.na(rownames(otu_table(physeq))))
taxa_are_rows(physeq)
any(rownames(otu_table(physeq)) == "")
any(duplicated(rownames(otu_table(physeq))))



MicroEco Package (pros & cons)
This is a package made specifically for microbial ecology analyses. It can be helpful for specific visualizations, although it has its limitations. It involves creating a microtable object and requires edits to that object.

mt <- microtable$new(sample_table = raref.metadat, otu_table = asv.table, tax_table = red.taxon)
mt

mt$tidy_dataset()
mt

# Example subset
mtsub <- clone(mt)
mtsub$sample_table <- subset(mtsub$sample_table, Day %in% c("1", "28"))
mtsub$tidy_dataset()

title: Data exploration & quality control
text:
QC

Checking sparsity
Microbiome datasets are usually sparse and have an uneven library size.

#check the number of zeros in the OTU table
sum(asv_count.df == 0)

#check the percentage of zeros in the OTU table
sum(asv_count.df == 0) / (nb_var * nb_samples) * 100







Discussion point




What is the meaning of a zero value in an OTU table?
Can we consider it to be a true zero?
Do you think it is important to filter the data and why?









Answers






A zero value in the OTU table means that we could not sequence any read for a specific OTU/ASV in a given sample. This means that there is not such OTU/ASV in the given sample or that the sequencing depth was not enough to find it.
So, we usually don’t know if it is a true zero or not.
First, some statistical approaches cannot handle highly sparse data set (for example Principal Component Analysis). Then, there is often problem when we have to compare rare OTU/ASV. For example, if for one sample you cannot find any count for a specific OTU but for another sample you can find 1 count for this OTU, can you say that there is more of this OTU in the second sample than in the first one? Therefore, in the context of microbiota data analysis, zeros values can be difficult to analyse and interpret and data should often be filtered.






Visualize the OTU count frequency
[histogram]


Get the minimum total OTU count over all samples

min(colSums(asv_count.df))



Check the number of non-zero values per OTU

non_zero <- 0*1:nb_var

for (i in 1:nb_var){
  non_zero[i]<-sum(asv_count.df[,i] != 0)
  }

plot(non_zero, xlab = "OTU", ylab = "Frequency", main = "Number of non zero values", las = 1)



Check the sequencing depth
Discuss Q: why do you think it is important to look for sequencing depth? First, important to know if we sequenced enough to capture all the diversity present in t our environment. Then, to compare samples to each other, we need to have a comparable library size between samples.


Rarefaction curve

rarecurve(asv_count.df, step = 100, cex = 0.75, las = 1) 



Library size

sum_seq <- rowSums(asv_count.df)
plot(sum_seq, ylim=c(0,25000), main=c("Number of counts per sample"), xlab=c("Samples"))
sum_seq

min(sum_seq)
max(sum_seq)

Q: how do you interpret these results; Do you think it is an issue to have variation in the library size?
[Of course if you want to compare samples to each other, it will be an issue to have different library sizes. For example, if you have a sample 1 with 1000 reads (500 reads for OTU1, 300 reads for OTU 2 and 200 reads for OTU 3) and a sample 2 with only 100 reads (50 reads for OTU1, 30 reads for OTU 2 and 20 reads for OTU 3). If you are comparing the two samples without correcting for the library size, you will say that sample 2 as 10 times less OTU 1, 2 and 3 than the sample 1, while it is just due to the difference in library size. Indeed, if you calculate the percentage, you will have 50% of OTU 1, 30% of OTU 2 and 20% of OTU 3 for both samples. So, > > it is important to normalize your data per sample.]


Standardizing abundances to the median sequencing depth

#standardize abundances to the median sequencing depth (https://joey711.github.io/phyloseq/preprocess.html)
total <- median(sample_sums(ps))
standf <- function(x, t=total) round(t * (x / sum(x)))
ps_normalized <- transform_sample_counts(ps, standf)

The taxonomy table
The taxonomy table (taxa.df) represents the assignment for the different OTU at domain, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species levels. Usually, microbial ecologists use phylum level (or class level for Proteobacteria) to describe the global bacterial communities. Then, they usually use OTU, ASV (Amplicon Sequence Variant) or genus level to check which bacteria are differentially occuring in the different treatments.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Getting started with RStudio
R is a programming language. In this workshop, we’re going to be working in RStudio, an Integrated Development Environment that lets us easily write and edit code.






RStudio interface
The RStudio user interface has 4 primary panes:

Source pane: allows you to view and edit various code-related files.
Console pane: provides an area to interactively execute code.
Environment pane: displays currently saved R objects.
Output pane: contains the Files, Plots, Packages, and Help tabs.

title: Introduction to R
text:
R basics

Creating a code document
Before we start working with code, we want to create a document we can save it in! This can be as basic as a .R document that just has code inside it.
We recommend that you try making a .qmd document. Quarto is an awesome tool & this document format lets you see the images you create & write text around your code to create reports and other output types:
File > New File > Quarto Document
Copy and paste the code from this document into your script and run it to follow along.


Running code
There are a few ways to run code:

Click the line and select CTRL + ENTER
Highlight the line and select CTRL + ENTER
Click the line and click ‘Run’ in the top menu bar
In a R or Quarto Markdown document, you can click the green ‘play’ button to run all of the code in the current chunk. Code chunks run from ```{r} to the next ``` . Each chunk should have a unique name.

You can also copy and paste (or type) code directly into the console pane after the ‘>’ prompt. Select ENTER to run the code.


Using functions
To make something happen in R, you use a function. For example, the sqrt function calculates the square root of a given number. To use a function, you’ll need to write it’s name with parentheses.
The inputs you give a function go inside those parentheses - these are called arguments.
For example, we can use the sqrt() function to calculate the square root of 256, by providing that number as our argument.
Try copy and paste this into your code document and run it to see the output.

sqrt(256)

[1] 16


In it’s simplest form, R code works like this:
object <- function(argument)
where:

an object holds a value e.g., the output of a function, a dataframe, a list.
the left arrow operator <- assigns a value.
A function does something e.g., performs a calculation, plots observations.
An argument is an input or parameter e.g., the data or a setting you want to use.



Installing and loading packages
R comes prepackaged with some default functions. You can install packages to get access to new collections of functions.
We can install new packages using the install.packages() function.
We only need to download and install a package once.

#Many popular R packages are hosted on CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network)
#these can be installed with the install.packages() function
install.packages("tidyverse")

However, every time we open RStudio, we need to load the packages we want to use in that session using the library() function.

library(tidyverse)



Creating objects
If you want to use the output of R functions later, you’ll need to save them. In R, you can save outputs and results by creating an object.
To create an object, type a name for the object and use the <- arrow to store a value in the object. You can call this literally anything you like, so long as it’s one string of characters.

my_favourite_number <- 256
my_favourite_number #this object holds the value '256'

sqrt(my_favourite_number)

my_new_favourite_number <- sqrt(my_favourite_number) #what value is stored in this new object?



Putting it all together to create aRt
Let’s install and load the flametree package to create a some tree aRt!

install.packages("flametree") #installing an R package that makes tree images
library(flametree) #loading the package

Create your beautiful aRt (R art):

#using the flametree_grow() and flametree_plot() functions to generate a tree image
my_beautiful_art <- flametree_grow(time=7, trees=15) %>%
  flametree_plot(background="gray10",
  palette=c("antiquewhite","coral","cyan4","goldenrod"),
  style="nativeflora") 

#let's take a look at the plot object we generated
my_beautiful_art








Once you’ve run this code, see what happens when:

You change the names of the colours in the palette argument. You can find a list of R colour names online, alongside a number of colour palette packages like RColorBrewer, viridis, and more. This tree is based on a Wes Anderson-inspired colour palette. Make sure colour names go inside quotation marks e.g., "forestgreen".
You change the tree style e.g., to “wisp” or “voronoi”.
You change the numeric value of the tree parameter.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Creating plots with ggplot

Introducing the Palmer penguins
The Palmer penguins dataset contains size measurements for three penguin species observed on three islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.
This data was collected from 2007 to 2009 by the US Long Term Ecological Research Network.







Creating a document
Before we start working on our code, we want to create an .qmd document we can save it in!
File > New File > Quarto Document
To make sure your code is reproducible, it’s good practice to load all the packages you need at the start of your document, using the library() function.

install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)

install.packages("palmerpenguins")
library(palmerpenguins)

Tidyverse is a collection of packages used for data manipulation, filtering, and visualization. Today, we’ll use functions from tidyverse to import data and create some plots.


Taking a look at our penguin data
Let’s take a look at our new data object.

#the head() function shows us the first 6 rows of data
head(penguins)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA          NA
5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


We can also use the glimpse() function to take a look at this object.

#the glimpse() function shows us the variables and what type of data they are (e.g., numeric or character strings)
glimpse(penguins)

Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species           <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adel…
$ island            <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgerse…
$ bill_length_mm    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, …
$ bill_depth_mm     <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, …
$ flipper_length_mm <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186…
$ body_mass_g       <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, …
$ sex               <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male…
$ year              <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…




Removing N/A values with drop_na()
We can see some N/A values in the raw data above. We can remove these with the drop_na() function.






penguins_nafree <- drop_na(penguins)
glimpse(penguins_nafree)

Rows: 333
Columns: 8
$ species           <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adel…
$ island            <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgerse…
$ bill_length_mm    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 41.1, 38.6…
$ bill_depth_mm     <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 17.6, 21.2…
$ flipper_length_mm <int> 181, 186, 195, 193, 190, 181, 195, 182, 191, 198, 18…
$ body_mass_g       <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3200, 3800…
$ sex               <fct> male, female, female, female, male, female, male, fe…
$ year              <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…


We can see that the NA values are gone, and 11 rows have been removed!


Creating plots with ggplot2
ggplot() is a function that creates plots.
Like a piece of art, we start with a base canvas where we set up our framework. We then use a + symbol to add layers on top.







ggplot() components
Every ggplot has three components:

data - your filtered data, ready for visualisation.
aesthetic mappings - this defines which variables we plot.
geom layer(s) - this defines how we visualise the observations.













Example: creating a scatterplot
Creating the base:

#setting the x and y axis variables
ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm))








Adding a geom layer with geom_point():

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) #geom_point() creates a scatterplot








Specifying point colour and shape:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species),size = 2)








Adding a custom colour palette:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species),size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"))








Adding custom axis labels:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species),size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4")) +
  labs(x="Bill length (mm)", y="Bill depth (mm)", color = "Penguin species", shape = "Penguin species")








Adding a theme:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species),size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4")) +
  labs(x="Bill length (mm)", y="Bill depth (mm)", color = "Penguin species", shape = "Penguin species") +
  theme_classic() #applying the classic theme to remove the background










Example: creating a boxplot
Creating the base:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm))








Adding a geom layer with geom_boxplot():

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot()








Specifying the boxplot (outline) colour:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(color=species)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") 








Specifying the boxplot (fill) colour:

#'alpha' sets the fill transparency to 50%
ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(color=species, fill=species), alpha=0.5) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") 








Adding axis labels:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(color=species, fill=species), alpha=0.5)+ 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") +
  labs(x="Penguin species", y="Flipper length (mm)") 








Adding jitter points:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(color=species, fill=species), alpha=0.5) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") +
  labs(x="Penguin species", y="Flipper length (mm)") +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.5)








Adding a theme:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(color=species, fill=species), alpha=0.5) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange","darkorchid","cyan4"), name = "Species") +
  labs(x="Penguin species", y="Flipper length (mm)") +

Creating the base:

ggplot(data = penguins_nafree, aes(x = species))








Adding a geom layer with geom_bar():

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Today’s tutorial follows the dada2 pipeline tutorial, where we’ll use the Divisive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm (DADA) to correct amplicon errors and assign taxonomy to amplicon sequence variants (ASVs).
Our starting point is a set of Illumina-sequenced, paired-end fastq files that have been split (or “demultiplexed”) by sample and from which the barcodes have been removed.
From this ‘raw’ microbiome sequencing data, the end products will be:

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table which records the numbers of times each exact amplicon sequence variant was observed in each sample.
A taxonomy table which records the taxonomic assignments for each ASV.

We will then export the ASV count table and taxonomy table for analysis.


By the end of today’s session, you should be able to:

Describe what an amplicon sequencing variant is
Evaluate why we need to control for sequencing errors
Apply the DADA2 pipeline steps to your own datasets

text:
Getting started in R

Installing and loading required packages
First we’ll load the required packages, including dada2. If you don’t already have these packages, see the Set-up instructions.

#load the necessary packages
library(dada2)
library(Rcpp)
library(ShortRead)
library(Biostrings)



Setting your working directory
Next, we’ll set our working directory - this tells R where on your computer you want it to look for files, and where you want to save files to. Make a folder with an intuitive name, like ‘MicrobiomeAnalysisWorkshop’, to serve as your working directory. Make sure that this is where all of the data files are saved.
You can do this by pasting the path to your folder into the code below, or from the menu: Session > Set Working Directory > Choose Directory… (CTRL + SHIFT + H).

#change this path to match your folder's location
setwd("/Users/myname/folder1/subfolder2/MicrobiomeAnalysisWorkshop")

#check your working directory location
getwd()

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Processing your sequencing reads

Assessing the quality of your .fastq reads
The FASTQ format stores experimental sequence measurements produced by a sequencing instrument. It can be thought of as FASTA, where every base has an associated quality score (hence FASTQ).
A typical single FASTQ read will have four sections:

A header (@) followed by an ID.
The nucleotide sequence.
A header (+) followed by an ID.
The last line encodes the quality scores for the sequences in section 2 (and should be the exact same length).

Below is an example of a high quality FASTQ read. Here, the header line includes a read ID and the length of the sequence.
@SRR1553607.1 1 length=202 
GTTAGCGTTGTTGATCGCGACGCAACAACTGGTAAAGAATCTGGAAGAAGGATATCAGTTCAAACGCTCAAG
+SRR1553607.1 1 length=202
BB@FFFFFHHHHHJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJGHIJJJJJJJJJHHHHHFFFFFEEEEEEEEEDDDDDDDDD
And here a low quality FASTQ read:
@SEQ_ID
GATTTGGGGTTCAAAGCAGTATCGATCAAATAGTAAATCCATTTGTTCAACTCACAGTTT
+SEQ_ID
!''*((((***+))%%%++)(%%%%).1***-+*''))**55CCF>>>>>>CCCCCCC65
Typically, when qualities look like “swearing” in a comic book (!@#$%^&*), it means that the data is low quality.

We can use fastQC to check the quality of our sequencing reads before we proceed with analysis. You can either run fastQC as an application on your computer, or as a tool in the command line. This tool will generate a report that lets us assess the quality of our sequencing data.
FastQC has a really well documented manual page with detailed explanations about every plot in the report. Examples of good and bad fastQC reports can also be found on the project website.


Importing your .fastq files
First we’ll define the path object so it points to the folder containing only the raw sequence read files. Then, we’ll read in the names of the fastq files & perform some string manipulation to get lists of the forward and reverse fastq files in matched order.

#assign path to sequencing .fastq files
path <- "/Users/myname/folder1/subfolder2/MicrobiomeAnalysisWorkshop/fastq"

#check which files are in this directory path
list.files(path)

#read in the names of the fastq files
fnFs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R1_001.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))
fnRs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R2_001.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))

#extract sample names, assuming filenames have format: SAMPLENAME_XXX.fastq.gz
sample.names <- gsub("_S.*", "", basename(fnFs))

#check the sample names
sample.names







Considerations for your own data



The string manipulations (which assume a SAMPLENAME_R1_001.fastq.gz file naming convention) may have to be modified if your filename format is different.








Adjustments for iSeq100 (2 x 150 bp) sequences





Read in the forward reads only. For all future steps, only run code for the forward reads.
The iSeq100 processes 2 x 150 base pair (bp) sequences - 1 forward and 1 reverse read, totaling 300 bp. The target sequence length for the 16S rRNA V4 region can vary from 250-350 bp. This means that the forward and reverse reads from the iSeq100 are too short to overlap for V4 sequences longer than 250 bp.
The DADA2 filtering and merging steps requires overlap between the forward and reverse reads to create a full sequence of the target region (16S rRNA V4). This is not possible with the 150 bp reads generated by the iSeq100. Therefore, we can only process the forward read (150 bp). Forward reads are typically higher quality than reverse reads (as you’ll likely see in the read quality profiles below). Although a 150 bp sequence provides less taxonomic resolution than the full 250-350 bp V4 sequence, this is still sufficient to assign taxonomy to our sequences.









Adjustments for long-read sequences





If you are working with PacBio reads, there is a DADA2 + PacBio pipeline available.
There are varying schools of thought around whether it is appropriate to assign amplicon sequencing variants to use Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing data with DADA2. This is primarily because of the higher error rates associated with older sequencing chemistry and basecalling models when this platform was first released. Circa 2024, ONT sequencing has been able to produce data with quality scores corresponding to >10% error-free reads or may not make it suited for the DADA2 workflow.
Similar to the iSeq workflow, you would process your singular read file (rather than two paired-end read files) and would change your minLen and maxLen parameters accordingly.
We would recommend that you investigate taxonomic assignment workflows which have been explicitly developed for error-prone long reads, including the epi2me metagenomics workflow and emu.





Examining read quality
We’ll start by visualizing the quality profiles of the forward reads:

plotQualityProfile(fnFs[3:4])








In gray-scale is a heat map of the frequency of each quality score at each base position. The mean quality score at each position is shown by the green line, and the quartiles of the quality score distribution are shown by the orange lines.
These forward reads are of good quality. We generally suggest you trim the last few nucleotides to avoid errors and reduced quality that can arise at the end of a sequence (after >200 cycles). These quality profiles do not suggest that any additional trimming is needed. We will truncate the forward reads at position 240 (trimming the last 10 nucleotides).
Now we visualize the quality profile of the reverse reads:

plotQualityProfile(fnRs[3:4])








It’s common for Illumina sequencing to produce reverse reads that are of lower quality - especially at the end. This isn’t too worrisome, as DADA2 incorporates quality information into its error model which makes the algorithm robust to lower quality sequence. However, trimming where the average qualities crash will improve the algorithm’s sensitivity to rare sequence variants. Based on these profiles, we will truncate the reverse reads at position 160 where the quality distribution crashes.






Considerations for your own data



Your reads must still overlap after truncation in order to merge them later! This tutorial is using 2 x 250 bp V4 sequence data, so the forward and reverse reads almost completely overlap and our trimming can be completely guided by the quality scores.
If you are using a less-overlapping primer set, like V1-V2 or V3-V4, your truncLen must be large enough to maintain 20 + biological.length.variation nucleotides of overlap between them




Filtering and trimming your data
First, we’ll assign new file names for the filtered .fastq.gz files we’re about to create.

filtFs <- file.path(path, paste0(sample.names, "_F_filt.fastq.gz"))
filtRs <- file.path(path, paste0(sample.names, "_R_filt.fastq.gz"))
names(filtFs) <- sample.names
names(filtRs) <- sample.names

To trim our data, we’ll use standard filtering parameters:

truncLen=c(200,200) : truncLen determines the cut-off length (in base pairs) for the forward and reverse reads.
maxN=0: DADA2 requires reads that have no Ns. This discards any read containing an ambiguous base.
rm.phix=TRUE: PhiX is a small phage originally isolated from E. coli and it’s DNA is commonly spiked in to Illumina sequencing libraries as a control. This parameter removes PhiX control reads.
maxEE=2: The maxEE parameter sets the maximum number of “expected errors” allowed in a read, which is a better filter than simply averaging quality scores. This discards any read with more than two expected errors.
truncQ=2: This truncates a read at the first base with a quality score ≤ 2.
multithread: This should be set to FALSE for Windows Operating Systems, or to TRUE for others.
compress=TRUE: This parameter saves filtered FASTQ files in a compressed (.gz) format.


out <- filterAndTrim(fnFs, filtFs, fnRs, filtRs, truncLen= c(200,200),
                     maxN=0, maxEE=c(2,2), truncQ=2, rm.phix=TRUE,
                     compress=TRUE, multithread=FALSE) #on Windows, set multithread=FALSE

head(out)

                               reads.in reads.out
1BFlemo_1A_S21_R1_001.fastq.gz    40070     39519
1BFlemo_1N_S45_R1_001.fastq.gz    47211     44884
1BSWR_1A_S13_R1_001.fastq.gz      12585     12306
1BSWR_1N_S37_R1_001.fastq.gz      88812     85605
1KFlemo_1A_S9_R1_001.fastq.gz     35782     34442
1KFlemo_1N_S33_R1_001.fastq.gz    36978     35916








Considerations for your own data



The standard filtering parameters are starting points, not set in stone. If you want to speed up downstream computation, consider tightening maxEE. If too few reads are passing the filter, consider relaxing maxEE, perhaps especially on the reverse reads (eg. maxEE=c(2,5)), and reducing the truncLen to remove low quality tails. Remember though, when choosing truncLen for paired-end reads you must maintain overlap after truncation in order to merge them later.
For ITS sequencing, it is usually undesirable to truncate reads to a fixed length due to the large length variation at that locus. That is OK, just leave out truncLen. See the DADA2 ITS workflow for more information.








Adjustments for iSeq100 (2 x 150 bp) sequences






out <- filterAndTrim(fnFs, filtFs, truncLen= 0,
                     maxN=0, maxEE=2, truncQ=2, rm.phix=TRUE,
                    compress=TRUE, multithread=TRUE) #on Windows, set multithread=FALSE (only needed for filterAndTrim)

head(out)

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Denoising
DADA2 attempts to provide the most accurate possible reconstruction of the exact amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) truly present in a sample from the noisy amplicon sequencing reads this process is called denoising. Achieving high accuracy in DADA2 requires both high sensitivity (i.e. reporting as many real ASVs as possible) and specificity (i.e. not reporting out spurious amplicon errors).
Denoising consists of two parts:

Classifying reads as error-free, or not.
Mapping error-containing reads to the appropriate error-free ASV.


Learning the error rates
Every amplicon dataset has a different set of error rates. The learnErrors function estimates the sequencing error rate from your dataset to try and distinguish sequencing errors from true sequence variants (i.e., ASVs).

#learn errors
errF <- learnErrors(filtFs, multithread=TRUE)
errR <- learnErrors(filtRs, multithread=TRUE)

It is always worthwhile (as a sanity check, if nothing else) to visualize the estimated error rates.

plotErrors(errF, nominalQ=TRUE)

Warning in scale_y_log10(): log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.
log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.









The error rates for each possible transition (A→C, A→G, …) are shown. Points are the observed error rates for each consensus quality score. The black line shows the estimated error rates after convergence of the machine-learning algorithm. The red line shows the error rates expected under the nominal definition of the Q-score. The estimated error rates (black line) should be a good fit to the observed rates (points), and the error rates should drop with increased quality.


Inferring sequence variants

#infer real sequence variants (denoised by taking the error rate into account)
dadaFs <- dada(filtFs, err=errF, multithread=TRUE)

Merging paired reads

Considerations for your own data



Most of your reads should successfully merge. If that is not the case upstream parameters may need to be revisited: Did you trim away the overlap between your reads?








Adjustments for iSeq100 (2 x 150 bp) sequences






# Merge dadaFs and filtFs
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaFs, filtFs, verbose=TRUE)
head(mergers)










Adjustments for ITS sequencing





For ITS sequences, you should increase the minimum overlap required between the forward and reverse reads, as ITS regions are more variable in length.

#merge paired reads
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaFs, filtFs, dadaRs, filtRs, minOverlap=20, maxMismatch=0, verbose=TRUE)
head(mergers)






Creating the ASV table
We can now construct an ASV table. The sequence table is a matrix with rows corresponding to (and named by) the samples, and columns corresponding to (and named by) the sequence variants.
This step filters out reads with lengths much smaller or larger than our target read length (~250-350 bp). The first step counts the occurrence of different read lengths in a table format. The second step allows you to trim sequence reads that are much shorter or larger than the read length with the highest counts.

#construct ASV sequence table
seqtab <- makeSequenceTable(mergers)

#inspect distribution of sequence lengths
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab)))


  204   220   259   260   261   262   267   290   291   292   293   294   295

  296   299   306   315 
   12     4     1     1 

#filter out reads larger or smaller than our target read length
seqtab2 <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 260:296]







Considerations for your own data



Sequences that are much longer or shorter than expected may be the result of non-specific priming. You can remove non-target-length sequences from your sequence table (eg. seqtab2 <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 250:256]). This is analogous to “cutting a band” out of a gel to get amplicons of the targeted length.








Adjustments for ITS sequencing





For ITS sequences, you should increase the allowed range of sequence lengths due to variability.

#merge paired reads
seqtab2 <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 200:500] 






Removing chimeras
Chimeras are not true sequence variants, but rather an artifact of the amplification process. Chimeras are ‘false’ DNA sequences formed by two or more biological sequences incorrectly joined together. Kind of like the mythological creature…

This often occurs during PCR reactions using mixed templates (e.g., environmental samples). Incomplete extensions during PCR allow subsequent PCR cycles to use a partially extended strand to bind to the template of a different, but similar, sequence. This partially extended strand then acts as a primer to extend and form a chimeric sequence. Once created, the chimeric sequence is then further amplified in subsequent cycles. The end result is a PCR artifact that does not represent a sequence that exists in nature.
Chimeric sequences can be identified if they can be exactly reconstructed by combining a left-segment and a right-segment from two more abundant “parent” sequences.

#remove chimeras
seqtab.nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seqtab2, method="consensus", multithread=TRUE, verbose=TRUE)

Identified 9251 bimeras out of 12180 input sequences.

#calculate the percentage of sequences that are non-chimeric
sum(seqtab.nochim)/sum(seqtab2)

[1] 0.4571335








Considerations for your own data



The frequency of chimeric sequences varies substantially from dataset to dataset, and depends on on factors including experimental procedures and sample complexity.
Most of your reads should remain after chimera removal (it is not uncommon for a majority of sequence variants to be removed though). If most of your reads were removed as chimeric, upstream processing may need to be revisited.
In most cases, this is caused by primer sequences with ambiguous nucleotides that were not removed prior to beginning the DADA2 pipeline. If you see over 25% of your sequencing reads being flagged as chimeric, trim the primers from your sequencing reads and restart the workflow.

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
section: Checkpoint: tracking reads through the pipeline
text:
Checkpoint: tracking reads through the pipeline
As a final check of our progress, we’ll look at the number of reads that made it through each step in the pipeline:

getN <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))
track <- cbind(out, sapply(dadaFs, getN), sapply(dadaRs, getN), sapply(mergers, getN), rowSums(seqtab.nochim))
# If processing a single sample, remove the sapply calls: e.g. replace sapply(dadaFs, getN) with getN(dadaFs)
colnames(track) <- c("input", "filtered", "denoisedF", "denoisedR", "merged", "nonchim")
rownames(track) <- sample.names
head(track)







Considerations for your own data



This is a great place to do a last sanity check. Outside of filtering, there should no step in which a majority of reads are lost. If a majority of reads failed to merge, you may need to revisit the truncLen parameter used in the filtering step and make sure that the truncated reads span your amplicon. If a majority of reads were removed as chimeric, you may need to revisit the removal of primers, as the ambiguous nucleotides in unremoved primers interfere with chimera identification.

If your reads do not seem to be appropriately assigned, for example lots of your bacterial 16S sequences are being assigned as Eukaryota NA NA NA NA NA, your reads may be in the opposite orientation as the reference database. Tell DADA2 to try the reverse-complement orientation with the argument tryRC=TRUE and see if this fixes the assignments.

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Saving your data
From our ‘raw’ microbiome sequencing data, we have produced the following end products:

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table (seqtab.nochim) which records the numbers of times each exact amplicon sequence variant was observed in each sample.
A taxonomy table (taxa) which records the taxonomic assignments for each ASV.

The most important thing to do at this stage is to save and export our data so we can analyze it later. Today we’ll export these tables to .txt files.

#make a copy of your final ASV table
asv_count.data <- seqtab.nochim

#check number of columns
ncol(asv_count.data)

#assign numbers to each column (i.e., each ASV), starting with ASV1
ASV_ID <- paste("ASV",sep = "",rep(1:ncol(asv_count.data)))

#replace the column names with ASV numbers
colnames(asv_count.data) <- ASV_ID

#export your ASV table to a file
write.table(asv_count.data, file="asv_count_table.txt")

# Export your ASV names and the associated taxonomy to a file
taxa.data <- cbind(ASV_ID,taxa)
write.table(taxa.data, file = "taxonomy_table.txt")

title: Data viz
text:
Calculating diversity indices
Two common diversity measures reported in microbiome studies are alpha and beta diversity:

Alpha diversity describes the species richness, evenness, or presence alone within a sample.
Beta-diversity measures compare the similarity of two or more communities.


Alpha diversity
Alpha diversity represents diversity within a sample. In other words, what is there and how much is there in terms of species. It is not always easy to define a species. Fortunately, we can calculate alpha diversity at different taxonomic levels. In this tutorial, we are looking at the ASV level.
Several alpha diversity indices can be calculated. Each index take into account different factors, which gives them unique advantages for assessing diversity within a sample:

Richness represents the total number of of distinct units observed within a sample. In our case, these are ASVs.
Chao1 estimates total richness. This prioritizes detection of rare species within a sample.
Pielou’s evenness provides information about the equity in species abundance in each sample. In other words, do all species have similar abundances, or do some species dominate?
Shannon index is based on richness & evenness and prioritizes spread of species within a sample.







Considerations around when to use raw or filtered data



Alpha diversity should be calculated from the raw ASV count data (rarefied_filtered_asv_count.data) and not from relative abundance data.
It is important to not use (numerically) filtered count data because many richness estimates are modeled on singletons and doubletons in the ASV count table. This means we need them to keep them in the dataset to meaningfully estimate richness.
Similarly, we typically do not use normalized data because we are not comparing samples to each other, but rather assessing diversity within each sample.
Note: these are really metrics to help contrast our samples within an experiment. Alpha diversity metrics should not be considered “true” values or be compared across studies.


Here, we are going to generate alpha-diversity plots following this tutorial.
Load the required packages and objects:

library(tidyverse)
library(vegan)
library(patchwork)
library(agricolae)
library(ggpubr)

#import our ASV, taxa, and metadata tables
rarefied_filtered_asv_count.data <- read.table(file="rarefied_filtered_asv_abundance_table.txt", sep = " ", header = TRUE,
                             quote = "\"", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

asv_relative_abundance.data <- read.table(file="relative_rarefied_filtered_asv_abundance_table.txt", sep = " ", header = TRUE,
                             quote = "\"", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

filtered_taxa.data <- read.table(file = "filtered_taxonomy_table.txt", sep = " ", header = TRUE,
                        quote = "\"", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

meta.data <- read.csv("sample_metadata.csv")



Calculating alpha diversity metrics
Here we are using the estimateR() and diversity() functions from the vegan package to calculate alpha diversity metrics.
Calculate richness: The estimateR() function estimates two richness types: bias-corrected Chao (Chiu et al., 2014)[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24945937/] and ACE (O’Hara 2005)[https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2656.2005.00940.x].
Calculate evenness: The diversity() function can be used to estimate evenness, Shannon, and Simpson diversity indices.


Rows: 18
Columns: 13
$ SampleID         <chr> "1BFlemo_1A", "1BFlemo_1N", "1BSWR_1A", "1BSWR_1N", "…
$ Oxygen_Level     <chr> "Aerobic", "Anaerobic", "Aerobic", "Anaerobic", "Aero…
$ Nutrient_Source  <chr> "Bone meal", "Bone meal", "Bone meal", "Bone meal", "…
$ Inoculant_Source <chr> "Flemo", "Flemo", "SWR", "SWR", "Flemo", "Flemo", "SW…
$ Steep_Time       <int> 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 28, 28, 28, 28, 28, 28, 28, 2…
$ S.obs            <dbl> 63, 101, 82, 210, 217, 240, 132, 318, 127, 94, 71, 10…
$ S.chao1          <dbl> 79.86667, 110.56250, 82.10000, 297.69231, 282.44231, …
$ se.chao1         <dbl> 9.2883337, 6.0366733, 0.3817756, 23.5903552, 18.84469…
$ S.ACE            <dbl> 114.29060, 110.03605, 82.48033, 314.08412, 275.04269,…
$ se.ACE           <dbl> 7.321330, 3.687589, 2.755152, 9.573733, 8.027222, 8.4…
$ alpha_evenness   <dbl> 0.8464758, 0.9486379, 0.9566284, 0.9473875, 0.9676465…
$ alpha_shannon    <dbl> 3.507063, 4.378078, 4.215593, 5.065783, 5.205839, 5.3…
$ alpha_simpson    <dbl> 0.961488, 0.985440, 0.982464, 0.991608, 0.993592, 0.9…




Visualizing alpha diversity metrics
Plot richness (number of species observed):

#plot the four alpha diversity indices
alpha_richness.plot <- ggplot(alpha_diversity, aes(x=Oxygen_Level, y=S.obs)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=Oxygen_Level)) + #add a boxplot
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#4477AA","#EE6677"), name="Oxygen level") + #custom colour palette and legend title
  geom_jitter(width=0.2) + #add points
  ylab("Observed richness") + #y axis label
  xlab("Oxygen level") + #x axis label
  theme_classic() #plot theme

alpha_richness.plot








Plot evenness:

alpha_evenness.plot <- ggplot(alpha_diversity, aes(x=Oxygen_Level, y=alpha_evenness)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=Oxygen_Level)) + #add a boxplot
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#4477AA","#EE6677"), name="Oxygen level") + #custom colour palette and legend title
  geom_jitter(width=0.2) + #add points
  ylab("Evenness") + #y axis label
  xlab("Oxygen level") + #x axis label
  theme_classic() #plot theme

alpha_evenness.plot








Plot Shannon diversity:

alpha_shannon.plot <- ggplot(alpha_diversity, aes(x=Oxygen_Level, y=alpha_shannon)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=Oxygen_Level)) + #add a boxplot
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#4477AA","#EE6677"), name="Oxygen level") + #custom colour palette and legend title
  geom_jitter(width=0.2) + #add points
  ylab("Shannon diversity") + #y axis label
  xlab("Oxygen level") + #x axis label
  theme_classic() #plot theme

alpha_shannon.plot








Plot Simpson diversity:

alpha_simpson.plot <- ggplot(alpha_diversity, aes(x=Oxygen_Level, y=alpha_simpson)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=Oxygen_Level)) + #add a boxplot
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#4477AA","#EE6677"), name="Oxygen level") + #custom colour palette and legend title
  geom_jitter(width=0.2) + #add points
  ylab("Simpson diversity") + #y axis label
  xlab("Oxygen level") + #x axis label
  theme_classic() #plot theme

alpha_simpson.plot














Discussion point




How many ASVs are observed across the different treatments?
How do you interpret the Evenness and Shannon plots?
Are there big differences between samples belonging to the same treatment? Are there big differences between treatments? How could you check this?





Statistical analyses

Checking the normality assumption
Now we’ll use statistical tests to test whether there are any significant differences between treatments. For this step, we’ll be looking at the Shannon diversity metric.
Before running significance tests, we need to know if data is normally distributed, which will tell use whether to use a parametric or non-parametric test. To test if the data are normally distributed, we will use the Shapiro-Wilk Normality test.

If the p-values are both not significant (p > 0.05) from the tests, we accept the null hypothesis (that the results are normally distributed) and test for significance between samples using parametric tests (e.g., (t-test)[https://www.datanovia.com/en/lessons/t-test-in-r/] and (ANOVA)[https://www.datanovia.com/en/lessons/anova-in-r/]).
summary(aov(metric ~ variable, data = alpha_diversity))
If the p-values are both significant (p < 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis (that the results are normally distributed) and test for significance between samples using non-parametric tests (e.g., (Wilcoxon)[https://www.datanovia.com/en/lessons/wilcoxon-test-in-r/] and (Kruskal-Wallis)[https://www.datanovia.com/en/lessons/kruskal-wallis-test-in-r/]).
kruskal.test(metric ~ variable, data = alpha_diversity)











    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  alpha_diversity$S.obs
W = 0.81482, p-value = 0.004314



    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  alpha_diversity$alpha_shannon
W = 0.96181, p-value = 0.6947



    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  alpha_diversity$alpha_simpson
W = 0.89843, p-value = 0.07584




Performing an omnibus test


             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
Oxygen_Level  1  0.836  0.8361   3.025  0.104
Residuals    14  3.870  0.2764               








Considerations for your own data




Is your data normally distributed?
Do any of your treatments or variables have an effect on alpha diversity?





Post-hoc tests
An omnibus test (e.g., ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis) may tell us that there is significant difference between the treatments, but we don’t know which treatment is significantly different from the others. In order to know what are the differences among the treatments/variable levels, we can perform a post-hoc test:

For normally distributed data, we can test for significance between samples using a parametric test (Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference).
TukeyHSD(metric_aov)
For data that is not normally distributed, we can test for significance between samples using a non-parametric test (e.g., Dunn, Nemenyi).







Considerations for your own data




How many levels does your variable of interest have? There is little use to performing a post-hoc test on a variable with only two levels…





Visualizing plots with statistics

alpha_shannon_stats.plot <- ggplot(alpha_diversity, aes(x=Oxygen_Level, y=alpha_shannon)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=Oxygen_Level)) + #add a boxplot
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("#4477AA","#EE6677"),
   name="Oxygen level") + #custom colour palette and legend title
  geom_jitter(width=0.2) + #add points
  ylab("Shannon diversity") + #y axis label
  xlab("Oxygen level") + #x axis label
  theme_classic() + #plot theme
  stat_compare_means(method = "anova",size=4,
   aes(label = paste0("ANOVA, p=", ..p.format..)), label.y=6) +
  geom_pwc(aes(group = Oxygen_Level), #add t-test
   tip.length = 0,
   method = "t_test", 
   label = "p.adj.format", p.adjust.method = "fdr") #p-adjustment helps limit false positives from multiple comparisons

alpha_shannon_stats.plot














Considerations for your own data



Using bullet points, write down everything you notice about the plots you produced.
What do you understand? What do you find confusing?
If you were going to publish these plots in a scientific paper, what features would you want to improve or add?
Now try plotting and running a statistical comparison for another variable. Adjust the necessary parameters and objects from the code above to assess a new variable’s levels. Which do you think may have the strongest impact on the final microbiome composition?





Beta diversity
While alpha-diversity represents the diversity within a sample, beta-diversity represents the difference between two samples. In other word, how similar or different are two samples?
Beta-diversity is a distance between two samples. Microbial ecologists do not use Euclidean distances. Bray-Curtis, Jaccard or weight/unweight Unifrac distances are more frequently to estimate the beta diversity:

Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is based on occurrence data (abundance).
Jaccard distance is based on presence/absence data (does not include abundance information).
UniFrac distances take into account the occurrence table and the phylogenetic diversity (sequence distance). Weighted or unweighted UniFrac distances depending if taking into account relative abundance or only presence/absence.

Distances metrics are between 0 and 1, where 0 means identical communities in both samples and 1 means different communities in both samples.






Considerations around when to use raw or filtered data



Beta diversity is calculated using filtered, normalized, and rarified data (rarefied_filtered_asv_count.data).


Calculate beta diversity:


           1BFlemo_1A 1BFlemo_1N 1BSWR_1A 1BSWR_1N 1KFlemo_1A
1BFlemo_1A      0.000      0.992    1.000    1.000      0.976
1BFlemo_1N      0.992      0.000    0.966    0.992      0.998
1BSWR_1A        1.000      0.966    0.000    0.876      1.000
1BSWR_1N        1.000      0.992    0.876    0.000      0.994
1KFlemo_1A      0.976      0.998    1.000    0.994      0.000



Visualizing high-dimensional data with ordination techniques
Ordinations techniques let us visualize high-dimensional data through dimensional reduction. In a nutshell, these techniques reduce high-dimensional data into a smaller number of dimensions so we can actually visualize them in 2D (or 3D). We can then compare samples based on relatedness.
The dimensions are whatever you’ve measured in each sample - in this case, these are our counts for each ASV.
There are several ordination techniques we could potentially use to do this:

Principal Components Analysis
non-metric multidimensional scaling (nMDS)

Today, we’re looking specifically at PCoA visualizations. Best practice would be to visualize your data by PCoA and nMDS.

#perform classic multidimensional scaling (cMDS)
bc_pcoa <- cmdscale(bc_dist,
                    k=(nrow(bc_dist)-1) #k is number of dimensions/ASVs - 1
                    , eig=TRUE) #eigenvalues will be generated

#store coordinates for first two principal components (PC) in new variable
bc_pc1and2 <- bc_pcoa$points[,1:2]

#store the eigenvalues in a new variable
bc_eigenvalue <- bc_pcoa$eig

#calculate the percentage of variance explained by PC1 and PC2
percent_explained <-bc_eigenvalue/(sum(bc_eigenvalue))*100
pe_PC1 <-percent_explained[1]
pe_PC2 <-percent_explained[2]

#report the percentage explained
print(paste0("PC1 explains ",signif(pe_PC1,3),"% of variance observed; PC2 explains ",signif(pe_PC2,3),"% of variance observed."))

[1] "PC1 explains 14.2% of variance observed; PC2 explains 11.9% of variance observed."

#create PCoA summary data
pcoa.data <- data.frame(
  Sample = rownames(bc_pc1and2),
  PCoA1 = bc_pc1and2[,1],
  PCoA2 = bc_pc1and2[,2],
  Oxygen_Level = meta.data$Oxygen_Level)

pcoa.plot <- ggplot(pcoa.data, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, color = Oxygen_Level, fill=Oxygen_Level)) +
 geom_point(aes(shape = Oxygen_Level), size = 3, stroke = 1) + #add a scatterplot
 scale_color_manual(values=c("grey", "#4477AA","#EE6677")) +
 scale_fill_manual(values=c("grey", "#4477AA","#EE6677")) +
  labs(x = paste0("PCoA1 (", round(pe_PC1, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", round(pe_PC2, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    color = "Oxygen Level", fill="Oxygen Level", shape="Oxygen Level") +
  theme_minimal() #theme with grid background
pcoa.plot














Stop & think




How do you interpret this plot?
What can you say about the total variance explained by this ordination?
What can you say about intra- and inter-group variability?









Considerations for your data



If you want to run an analysis on a subset of your data, you must re-calculate your beta diversity index from the first step.




Statistical analysis
To test whether the groups are different with respect to centroid and dispersion, a PERMANOVA statistical test will be performed. For this, a multi-variate extension of ANOVA will be used, as there are many ASVs that will be used in the test. The extension is based on distances between samples. The test compares distances of samples within the same group to distances of samples from different groups. If the distance between samples from the different groups is much larger than samples from the same group, we conclude that the groups are not equal.
In order to test the significance of the result, a permutation test is used - all samples are randomly mixed over the groups and the test is repeated many times. If the ratio (between group distance / within group distance) is much larger for the original data than for the permutations, we conclude there is a statistical significant difference.
The test can be applied in combination with any distance measure. Here we use the Bray-Curtis distance used for the PCoA above.
First, we will test if there is any significant effect of the treatment/variable:

# PERMANOVA test using the vegan package
adonis2(rarefied_filtered_asv_count.data~Oxygen_Level,data=meta.data, permutations=9999, method="bray")







Stop & think




How do you interpret this PERMANOVA result?
What can you say about intra- and inter-group variability?









Answers





If the P-value is less than 0.05, we can conclude that the intra-variability is lower than the inter-variability among the two groups and that we have a significant effect.

Bacterial composition plots
Cover some very common visualizations which you will also frequently encounter in the literature - barplots… In this part of the tutorial, you will learn how to plot and interpret microbiome composition.

# Combine the taxonomic table, data_taxo_filt_rar, with the new OTU table, data_otu_filt_rar_temp

dim(data_otu_taxo_filt_rar)

data_otu_taxo_filt_rar[1:5, 1:5]

title: Microbiome Data Analysis in R
text:
This workshop will introduce you to microbiome data analysis and guide you through how to process, analyse, and visualize microbial amplicon sequencing data.






Follow the instructions in the Set-up section to install the required packages and files.
Decide whether you want to use our practice data, or your own sequencing data.
Get comfortable - you will be following along in RStudio on your own computer!

title: Data exploration, normalization, & quality control
text:
So far, we have created two data tables using the DADA2 pipeline:

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table (asv_count.data) which records the numbers of times each exact amplicon sequence variant was observed in each sample.
A taxonomy table (taxa.data) which records the taxonomic assignments for each ASV.

We’ll also be working with a metadata table (meta.data) which represents metadata information for the different samples.
In this session, we will:

Examine these data tables.
Perform necessary quality control checks (e.g., sparsity and sequencing depth).
Filter & normalize our databy sample.



By the end of today’s session, you should be able to:

Examine and interpret the key features of ASV datasets.
Evaluate the quality of ASV datasets.
Perform data manipulation for quality control (and determine when this is appropriate).
crumbs: Day 2: Data exploration, normalization, & quality control

Filtering out unwanted ASVs
First, we will remove unwanted classifications or ASVs. This includes:

Unclassified sequences (with no taxonomy data).
Archaeal sequences.
Mitochondrial sequence contamination.
Chloroplastic sequence contamination (particularly when sampling microbiomes associated with plants).







Stop & think




The code below should remove ASVs classified as coming from chloroplasts and mitochondria.
These reads can show up in our 16S sequencing data because environmental samples can have DNA from non-microbial organisms, such as plant roots, leaves, or eukaryotic tissue.
16S rRNA amplicon sequencing amplifies DNA from chloroplasts and mitochondria because these organelles evolved from prokaryotic organisms (see: (the endosymbiosis theory)[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1369527414001283]).
The highly conserved regions of 16S serve as consistent targets for sequencing, but they are also highly conserved in non-target organelles, so we must filter out off-target kingdoms of life.

Stop & think




What is the meaning of a zero value in an ASV table?
Can we consider it to be a true zero?
Do you think it is important to filter the data and why?









Answers






A zero value in the ASV table means that we could not sequence any read for a specific ASV in a given sample. This means that the ASV is not present in the given sample, or that the sequencing depth was not enough to find it.
Because of this, we usually don’t know if it is a true zero or not.
The issue of whether something is truly absent (or not) is problematic, especially when we have to compare rare ASVs. Furthermore, some statistical approaches cannot handle highly sparse data set (e.g., Principal Component Analysis). For microbiome data analysis, zeros values can be difficult to analyse and interpret and data should be filtered if the percentage of zeros is relatively high.










Considerations for your own data




Microbial ecologists usually remove singletons (ASVs for which only one read has been identified in the full ASV table), as these are likely to be artifacts.
Be aware that some diversity metrics take these singletons into account, so you might not always want to remove them (e.g., Chao1 alpha diversity).
Another option for data filtering could be to remove ASVs that have a total count (per ASV, over all samples) lower than a defined value.
As a reminder, chimeric amplification products have been already removed in DADA2 pipeline.

Check how frequently ASVs are shared between samples:

non_zero <- 0*1:nb_var

for (i in 1:nb_var){
  non_zero[i]<-sum(filtered_asv_count.data[,i] != 0)
  }

plot(non_zero, xlab = "ASV", ylab = "Frequency", main = "Number of non zero values", las = 1)








It is likely that the majority of ASVs are found only in a few samples. In other words, very few ASVs will be found at high frequencies or across all samples.






Considerations for your own data



If you have replicate samples, you could think about filtering out rare ASVs that are not shared between at least 2 or 3 samples.




Checking the sequencing depth
Sequencing depth and library size represent the number of counts per sample. This number can vary a lot among the different samples (up to 10-fold).
Differences in library size can be due to technical biases or errors introduced when creating DNA sequencing libraries in the lab: - The PCR amplification step can introduce some difference among samples because PCR amplification can be more orless efficient according to the sequence itself. - After cleaning up PCR amplicons from each sample, we typically measure the DNA concentration. Depending on the method used (e.g., band brightness, NanoDrop, Qubit), this may not be a highly accurate or sensitive measure. - Then, according to these concentrations, we pool the different samples into one ‘equimolar’ mix, which can also introduce some error.






Stop & think



Why do you think it is important to look at sequencing depth?








Answers






It is important to know if we sequenced enough to capture all the diversity present in our environment.
To compare samples to each other, we need to have a comparable library size between samples.






Checking library size
Check the number of ASV counts per sample:

#calculate the number of counts per sample
library_size <- rowSums(filtered_asv_count.data)
summary(library_size)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    941    4274    9686   11630   14750   32135 

#check if any samples have zero counts
library_size[library_size == 0]

named numeric(0)

#plot the number of counts per sample as a histogram
plot(library_size, ylim=c(0,25000), main=c("Number of counts per sample"), xlab=c("Samples"))







#check the minimum library size
min(library_size)

[1] 941

#check the maximum library size
max(library_size)

[1] 32135








Considerations for your own data



Do your samples have differences in the library size? If you want to compare samples to each other (hint: you do), it will be an issue to have different library sizes. To fix this, we will normalize our library sizes.
If any of your samples have no counts at all, they should be removed from analysis.

title: Data exploration, normalization, & quality control
text:
Normalizing abundance data

Checking the rarefaction curve
We can explore sequencing depth though a rarefaction curve. The rarefaction curve shows how many new ASVs are observed when we obtain new reads for a given sample - essentially visualizing ASV richness across sampling depths.

rarecurve(filtered_asv_count.data, step = 100, cex = 0.75, las = 1, xlab="Number of reads", ylab = "Number of ASVs observed") 

Warning in rarecurve(filtered_asv_count.data, step = 100, cex = 0.75, las = 1,
: most observed count data have counts 1, but smallest count is 2









The key to interpreting these curves is to identify where ASV richness plateaus. If the sequencing depth is sufficient, we should observe a plateau. This means that even if we sequence new reads from that sample, they will belong to ASVs already observed. In other word, all the diversity present in a sample is already captured and we have sequenced the community deeply enough.
The sequencing depth at which ASV richness plateaus can serve as the cut-of point for normalization. This allows us to retain the maximum amount of ASV diversity, while creating even sequence depth across samples for downstream processing. Rarefying is ideal for beta diversity analyses.
Note: we cannot use rarefaction curves to estimate total richness of a sample - we primarily look at these as a general data vibe check.






Considerations for your own data



Do your samples reach a plateau? Does the total number of reads vary between samples?




Rarefying the abundance data


[1] 18


Warning in rrarefy(filtered_asv_count.data, 500): function should be used for
observed counts, but smallest count is 2

title: Data exploration, normalization, & quality control
text:
End products
From our ‘raw’ data tables, we have produced the following end products:

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table (rarefied_filtered_asv_count.data) which has:

Been filtered to remove unwanted ASVs
Been normalized to rarefy samples

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table (asv_relative_abundance.data) which has:

Been filtered to remove unwanted ASVs
Been normalized to rarefy samples
Had counts converted to relative abundance (%)

A taxonomy table (filtered_taxa.data) which records the taxonomic assignments for each ASV which has:

Been filtered to remove unwanted ASVs


The most important thing to do at this stage is to save and export our data so we can analyze it later.

#export your ASV table to a file
write.table(rarefied_filtered_asv_count.data, file="rarefied_filtered_asv_abundance_table.txt")

#export your ASV table to a file
write.table(asv_relative_abundance.data, file="relative_rarefied_filtered_asv_abundance_table.txt")

# Export your filtered taxonomy file to a file
write.table(filtered_taxa.data, file = "filtered_taxonomy_table.txt")

title: Data exploration, normalization, & quality control
text:
Other quality control considerations

Positive controls & mock data with DADA2


Negative controls
It is important to include negative controls throughout the extraction and amplification process. These can include blank samples that go through the extraction process, and no-template controls that go through the amplification process. These negatives can then be used to ensure these steps are not amplifying unwanted DNA from the laboratory environment

View(asv_relative_abundance.data) # Sample names as columns


Scroll to BLANK or NEG samples
Order from high to low to see counts for most abundant ASVs
Interpret:


Reads should be below 1000 per ASV
Sample should contain less than 100 different ASVs
If higher than these benchmarks, this could be problematic for interpreting ASVs in actual samples and further steps should be taken to account for these ASVs







Considerations for your own data



You can identify and even remove contaminants from your dataset with the decontam package.
